conversation.content:
Hello there—thank you for taking the time to meet with me. I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician, and my job is to check in on how moms are feeling emotionally after their baby arrives. Today I’ll be using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS for short. It’s a brief, 10-question screening that looks at mood, anxiety, and—just as important—any thoughts of self-harm that can sometimes pop up in the postpartum weeks. Everything you share stays between us unless there’s an immediate safety concern, and we’ll move at whatever pace feels comfortable.

I’ll ask each question conversationally, and all I need is the answer that best fits how you’ve felt in the past seven days—no right or wrong responses. Ready to start?

**Question 1:** In the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

Honestly, most of the time it feels pretty hard to laugh. My sister sent me a silly meme yesterday and I just stared at it—nothing felt funny. I used to laugh all the time before the baby came, but this week I barely cracked a smile.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not really… I mean, maybe once or twice something small made me smile, but it felt forced. Mostly I just feel flat, like the joy is stuck behind a wall.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not much. I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk, even a shower without interruption—but this week it all feels like one more chore. I still do the activities, but I’m just going through the motions.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that a lot. If the baby’s fussy, I immediately think it’s because I’m not soothing him right, or if I can’t get him to nap I’m sure it’s my fault for not reading his cues. I know rationally babies just cry sometimes, but in the moment I feel like I’m failing him.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding him and suddenly picture him choking, or I’ll lie down and imagine the crib sheet coming loose and covering his face. There’s no real reason—it’s just this constant buzz of “what if something happens?” I can usually talk myself down after a while, but it pops up over and over.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes, yeah. It’s like a sudden wave—my heart races and I feel shaky, even if everything’s quiet. Last night the baby was asleep, but I woke up gasping, sure something was wrong. It passed after a minute, but the feeling left me rattled.
Things have been getting on top of me

Mostly I can muddle through, but yes—there have definitely been moments this week when it all feels like too much. Yesterday the dishes were piled up, the baby wouldn’t nap unless I held him, and I just stood in the kitchen holding back tears, thinking, “I can’t do this.” I still got everything done eventually, but it felt like I was barely treading water.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes. I lie down exhausted, but my mind keeps circling—worrying I missed something, replaying every little sound the baby made, feeling guilty that I’m not happier. Some nights I drift off okay, then jolt awake for no reason and can’t settle again. It’s not every single night, but more often than not.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day this week. I wake up with this heavy feeling, like a gray cloud parked over me. Sometimes it lifts for a little while—usually when the baby smiles—but it settles right back in. I keep thinking, “I should be grateful,” but the sadness just sits there anyway.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… I’ve cried three or four times since last week. Nothing huge sets it off—just feeling overwhelmed or like I’m not doing enough. The other night I was folding tiny onesies and the tears started. I felt silly, but I couldn’t stop them.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I get down on myself, but I would never want to leave my baby or my family.

You've shared that this week has felt heavy-laughter and excitement seem distant, replaced by a flat, gray mood that settles in most days. You're working so hard to care for your baby, yet you often blame yourself when he fusses, and waves of worry or even panic arrive without warning. Sleep is fractured by racing thoughts, and tears come easily, though you're clear you would never want to leave your family. Your honesty shows strength, and these emotional shifts are common, treatable parts of new motherhood.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 22, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports almost no ability to laugh naturally and describes joy as inaccessible, aligning with "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports noticeably diminished enjoyment compared to her past, matching "Definitely less than I used to"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent self-blame for normal infant behaviors, indicating it occurs "most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports intrusive, recurrent anxiety "pretty much every day" with vivid catastrophic images, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden panic attacks that occur sometimes, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent coping struggles this week—feeling overwhelmed, tearful, and doubting ability to manage—aligning with "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent sleep disruption linked to unhappiness—"more often than not"—aligning with "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive daily sadness with only brief relief, matching 'Yes, most of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient reports multiple crying episodes in the past week triggered by feeling overwhelmed, matching 'Yes, quite often</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS total of 22 falls well above the 14-point cutoff indicating probable <med>major depressive episode with peripartum onset</med> and co-occurring <med>anxiety</med>. The patient endorses <sym>depressed mood</sym> and <sym>loss of interest</sym> most of the time, plus <sym>guilt</sym>, <sym>sleep disturbance</sym>, and <sym>feeling overwhelmed</sym>-all meeting <med>DSM-5 criteria</med> for depression. No self-harm ideation (Q10 = 0) lowers acute risk yet mood severity still warrants prompt evaluation. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Schedule urgent appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> within the next few days
2. Bring this EPDS result and share how daily functioning feels; ask about both therapy and medication options compatible with breastfeeding
3. Enlist practical support-partner, friend, or postpartum doula-to cover household tasks and allow 3-4 hour blocks of uninterrupted rest
4. Practice 5-minute grounding or breathing exercises when <sym>panic</sym> rises; keep lights dim and phone off if awakened at night to protect remaining sleep
5. Stay connected-text one supportive person each day; isolation can intensify <sym>low mood</sym>
6. Keep baby-safe hotlines handy: Postpartum Support International 1-800-944-4773 or 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline for 24/7 emotional support
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 22: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – Brief Professional Note  

Date: ___  
Source: Client self-report (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale–style interview)  

Presenting concerns endorsed  
• Persistent low mood, anhedonia, tearfulness (daily, >1 wk)  
• Excessive guilt / self-blame regarding infant care  
• Generalized anxiety & intrusive “what-if” fears about infant safety  
• Panicky episodes (heart racing, gasping awake) without clear trigger  
• Sleep disruption secondary to ruminating and middle-of-night awakenings  
• Feeling overwhelmed / “can’t do this”; chores feel unmanageable  

Pattern: Symptoms present most days, interfere with functioning, but no self-harm ideation reported (“never”).  

Screening significance  
– Meets threshold indicators for possible Major Depressive Episode with peripartum onset and co-occurring anxiety.  
– Absence of self-harm ideation lowers acute safety risk; continue routine monitoring.  

Next steps (screening only)  
Recommend formal clinical interview (DSM-5-TR) and standardized rating scales; evaluate social supports; consider medical causes for mood/sleep disturbance; provide psycho-education and crisis resources.
